conflict_topics: Tent placement blocking lift / wheelchair access
Noise from chanting interfering with night-shift sleep
Morning exercise spot and shade (competing daytime use)
Logistics of moving/maintaining tent and speaker orientation
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants gave concrete reasons and practical constraints (wheelchair access, night-shift sleep, need for shade for daytime wake, morning exercise under shade).
Multiple specific, implementable proposals were offered: move tent, point speakers away, change exercise time to 6:30.
Agents accepted or declined with explicit, contextual reasons rather than empty politeness.
Closure included mutual confirmations rather than unilateral promises.
evaluation.final_reason: Conflicts were settled by concrete, mutual accommodations: Agent D agreed to shift the tent to allow Agent A's mother wheelchair access ('We can definitely shift it to make sure there's enough space.' — Turn 2) and to direct speakers away from the block to address Agent B's sleep ('I'll make sure we point them away from the block.' — Turn 17). Agent C agreed to use the other open area in the morning and start earlier ('what if my group uses the open area and we just start earlier? Say 6:30?' — Turn 19) and confirmed 'We can manage for a few days.' (Turn 21). Those mutual, concrete acceptances resolved the remaining substantive incompatibilities.
position_change_notes: Agent D conceded on location and equipment orientation: agreed to shift the tent for wheelchair access and to point speakers away (Turn 2; Turn 17).
Agent C changed routine to accommodate the wake: proposed and confirmed earlier start at a different open area for a few days (Turn 19; Turn 21).
Agent B maintained the concern about sleep but accepted a technical mitigation (speaker direction) rather than demanding timing changes (Turn 6; Turn 16–17).
Agent A's request (clear space for wheelchair) was accepted early and did not require further change from A (Turn 1; Turn 25).

round_scores.evidence: Agent A raised a practical blockage: 'the tent... it's a bit in the way of the lift. My mother needs to get past with her wheelchair' (Turn 1). Agent D immediately agreed to shift it: 'We can definitely shift it to make sure there's enough space.' (Turn 2).

Agent B introduced a new, substantive incompatibility between the wake and his need to sleep on the night shift: 'I'm on the night shift tonight and Sunday. I have to sleep in the evenings, and the sound... it's going to be right at my window.' (Turn 4). No solution was offered yet.

Agent D asserted the ceremony's necessity and set a firm time: 'It's a really important part of the ceremony for my grandfather. We have to do it. The chanting should finish around 10:30 each night.' (Turn 5). This resists changes to timing and leaves B's sleep concern unresolved.

Agent C raised a separate spatial/temporal conflict: the tent occupies the spot used for morning exercise at 7 a.m.: 'the tent, it's in the space where we do our morning exercise. The aunties and uncles will be here at 7.' (Turn 7). Agent D did not yet settle this and asked to find a spot.

Agent B proposed moving the setup to the other open area: 'If the whole setup moves there, it's clear for the lift and the exercise spot, and it would be further from the windows.' (Turn 11). This is a proposal but not accepted yet; the underlying incompatibility (shade/morning exercise vs lift/window/noise) remains.

Agent D pushed back because the alternate spot lacks shade during the day: 'But Agent C just said that spot is very hot. We will be here all day, my family needs shade.' (Turn 12). The parties are maintaining incompatible practical needs (shade/daytime presence vs other uses).

Agent C pointed out the morning use problem remains and Agent D rejected moving back-and-forth: 'That might work for the evening chanting, but the tent would still be in our spot at 7 a.m.' (Turn 14). 'And we can't move the whole setup every evening and morning. The wake is for three days, my family and friends will be here in the daytime too.' (Turn 15). Positions hardened on practical constraints.

Agent B proposed a partial accommodation to address the noise issue: 'could the speakers just be pointed away from the building?' (Turn 16). Agent D accepted that concrete mitigation: 'I'll make sure we point them away from the block.' (Turn 17). B's sleep concern was defused, but the morning exercise/shade/location disagreement remained.

Agent C offered to change their morning routine: 'what if my group uses the open area and we just start earlier? Say 6:30?' (Turn 19). Agent D accepted: 'Are you sure? That would be a huge help... That's very kind of you' (Turn 20). C confirmed: 'We can manage for a few days.' (Turn 21). These exchanges produce a concrete, mutual agreement resolving the remaining spatial/temporal conflicts.
Confirmations and thanks only: Agent C 'We can manage for a few days.' (Turn 21). Agent B expressed appreciation (Turn 23). No substantive disagreement present.
Agent D checked that the tent shift solves A's access and Agent A confirmed: 'Yes, that's perfect.' (Turns 24–25). No outstanding substantive incompatibility.
Only expressions of gratitude and closure: 'Thank you, everyone... It means a lot to my family.' (Turn 29). No substantive disagreement.

substantive_insights: Temporal separation (morning vs evening) enabled compromises: morning exercisers moved earlier while evening chanting remained in place.
Small technical mitigations (pointing speakers away) resolved a noise problem without changing ceremonial timing.
Physical constraints (shade availability) were the core limit on relocating the tent, not unwillingness to cooperate.
Different needs required a mix of concessions across parties rather than a single unilateral change.
